sections.title: Page 1

summary.text: The cover page and opening note of a progress and evaluation report on the Expanded Programme on Immunization (EPI) for the World Health Assembly, explaining that it was updated after Executive Board discussion and that the programme's Global Advisory Group endorsed its proposed targets for the coming decade, including a plan of action to eradicate poliomyelitis. It also mentions an annex of tables on immunization coverage and on deaths and cases prevented, and lists the report's contents, though much of the Arabic OCR on this page is garbled.

sections.title: Page 2

summary.text: Opens the introduction by describing a quiet revolution in public health over the past fifteen years, as immunization services in developing countries grew from almost nothing to reach a large share of the world's children with measles, polio, DPT and BCG vaccines, preventing over a million deaths a year from measles, whooping cough and neonatal tetanus as well as many polio cases. A figure shows estimated immunization coverage of infants, and of pregnant women against tetanus, by WHO region.

sections.title: Page 3

summary.text: Notes that vaccine-preventable diseases still kill about three million children a year and disable many more, calls for coverage of at least 80% of children by 1990 and at least 90% by 2000 within maternal and child health services, and states that the report reviews the programme's experience and sets new goals for the next decade. It then traces the programme's basis in World Health Assembly resolutions since 1974, including the Alma-Ata Declaration and the 1988 decision to eradicate poliomyelitis by 2000, and describes how the EPI grew into a broad alliance of United Nations bodies, development agencies and voluntary groups.

summary.text: A figure page showing countries and areas with immunization coverage above or below a set level for the third dose of polio or DTP vaccine in children up to 12 months old in 1988, with the map itself lost in the OCR text.

sections.title: Page 5

summary.text: Describes the international financial support behind the EPI, with UNICEF as the main source of vaccines and equipment and further backing from bilateral and multilateral agencies, the World Bank, UNDP and private groups such as the Rockefeller Foundation and Rotary International, whose PolioPlus campaign raised funds mainly for polio vaccine. It outlines WHO's technical role, including an operations manual, training materials, an information system for global coverage and disease estimates, technical papers and the EPI newsletter, as well as its lead with UNICEF in improving cold-chain methods and equipment. It also notes joint WHO/UNICEF technical statements and work to strengthen national management, and UNICEF's social mobilization and advocacy through its annual State of the World's Children report.

sections.title: Page 6

summary.text: Continues with UNICEF's promotion of national immunization days after their success in Colombia and its 'We the Peoples' pledge, and the creation of the Task Force for Child Survival by WHO, UNICEF, the World Bank, UNDP and the Rockefeller Foundation after a meeting at Bellagio, with follow-up meetings at Cartagena and Talloires leading to the Talloires Declaration. It places immunization within primary health care as defined at Alma-Ata and describes links with diarrhoeal disease control, birth spacing, and vitamin A and iodine supplementation. It then opens the review of regional progress, noting that all WHO regions have advanced but that Europe and the Americas lead while Africa still has the largest share of infants with low coverage.

sections.title: Page 7

summary.text: Reviews the African Region, where immunization coverage is lower than elsewhere but rising quickly after the African Immunization Year, although third-dose DPT coverage remains low in several countries such as Ethiopia, Angola, Chad and Mali. It describes mixed fixed and outreach delivery strategies, the role of political and religious leaders and district health development, self-reliance policies such as the Bamako Initiative, staff training, programme evaluations and coverage surveys, and a standardized semi-annual reporting form and computerized information system agreed with UNICEF.

sections.extract: A42/10 1٠١/٥٤ ‏ج‎ صفحة 7 7 page 5-؟ وفي الاقليم الاأفريقي نجد أن التغطية بالتمنيع بمستضدات البرنامج الموسع للتمنيع ء باسكثناء الحصبة والبي سي جي » تقل كثيرا عنها في الاقاليم الاأخرى (الشكلان ‎١‏ و ؟) ‎٠‏ وكما أشير اليه في الفقرة ‎١-6‏ ء فان ذلك يعكس مستوى التنمية الاجتماعية الاقتصادية ومستوى تطور البنيات الأساسية الصحية في أفريقيا » غير أن التغطية تزداد بسرعة نتيجة المبادرات المتخذة خلال عام ١٩٨٦ والتي أسمتها اللجنة

sections.title: Page 8

summary.text: Continues the African Region review with preparations for poliomyelitis eradication, including country assessments, a regional round table and endorsement by the joint UNICEF/WHO technical group on immunization, and a regional committee resolution to eliminate neonatal tetanus supported by planning workshops. It also notes advice to add yellow fever vaccine to routine schedules in endemic countries and regional operational studies on the cold chain, new vaccines and missed opportunities. For the Region of the Americas, it describes progress towards immunizing all children and interrupting wild poliovirus transmission, coordinated agency support with five-year national plans of action, and national vaccination days held at least twice a year in polio-endemic countries.

sections.extract: A42/4210 1١/51 صفحة / 8 ع8هم 9-5 وقد شجتهت البلدان على صياغة المرامي من حيث الانخفاض في عدد حالات الاصابة بالاأمراض ‎٠‏ وشرعت عدة بلدان لديها برامج وطنية راسخة ونظم متطورة للترصد في توثيق هذه الانخفاضات ‎٠‏ ‎٠١-5‏ وتم الاضطلاع بعدد من الأنشطة التحضيرية في الاقليم من أجل استكصال التهاب سنجابية النخاع » وجرى تقييم الوضع في ‎٢٠‏ بلدا » واستعرضت الخدمات المختبرية في سبعة بلدان » وانعقدت "مائدة مستديرة " في المكتب

sections.title: Page 9

summary.text: Reports for the Americas that national vaccination days should complement rather than replace routine services, that weekly district-level poliomyelitis reporting, including reports of no cases, has strengthened surveillance, and that confirmed polio cases as well as measles and whooping cough have declined, with English-speaking Caribbean countries setting a goal to eliminate measles. It notes the neonatal tetanus cases reported each year and plans to focus control on the districts where they occur. For South-East Asia, it describes the computerized regional information system, country programme review meetings, growing attention to urban coverage, the need to involve curative facilities, and the importance of management and supervision training.

sections.extract: 4210 ٠. / ‏ج17‎ ضقحة 9 9 فهدهم الوطنية ‎٠‏ وينبغي اعتبار أيام التلقيح الوطنية مكملة لخدمات التمنيع المقدمة كجزء من الخدمات الصحية الأساسية لا بديلا عنها + وقد شوهدت نتائج ايجابية في عدة بلدان حيث زادت التغطية بالتمنيع باللقاح المضاد للحصبة واللقاح الثلاثي وانخفضت معدلات الانقطاع ‎٠‏ ك/1 وقطور الترصق بسرعة كما ان الككير من البلدان قد حسنت من توعية تظمهيا للمعلومات ‎٠‏ وكآان التركيز علسى الدائرة ‎٠‏ بوصفها الوحدة

sections.title: Page 10

summary.text: Reports rising government and external funding for immunization in the South-East Asia Region, broken down by source, and declining incidence of target diseases in several countries, while noting that measles coverage had been too low to affect illness. For the European Region, it describes wide variation in programme quality, formal cold-chain assessments, falling incidence of most target diseases but a rise in measles, and the planned or actual use of measles-mumps-rubella vaccine in many countries despite supply problems. It lists areas needing more regional support, stresses the plan to eradicate polio from Europe in light of a recent outbreak in Israel, and opens the Eastern Mediterranean section by noting increased coverage.

sections.extract: A42/10 5 / 1/4 صفحة ‎١٠‏ 0 ع28م أولوية عالية للتدريب على كل من الجوانب الادارية والتقنية لبرامج التمنيع في الاقليم وذلك من أجل تحسين الأداء في الأنشطة الأخرى للرعاية الصحية الأولية ‎٠‏ 5-5؟ وتشير البيانات المستمدة من نظام معلومات البرنامج الموسع للتمنيع الى أن هناك زيادة في المساهمات المقدمة من الحكومات ومن المصادر الخارجية منذ عام 11/80 ووصل مجموع الأموال المتوافرة الى ‎١٩‏ مليون دولار أمريكي في عام ١٩٨٥ والى ‎١‏

sections.title: Page 11

summary.text: Describes progress in the Eastern Mediterranean Region through integration with primary health care, intersectoral cooperation and social mobilization, special help for the slowest-progressing countries affected by conflict and economic hardship (Afghanistan, Sudan, Somalia and the two Yemens), the continuing heavy toll of neonatal tetanus, and a regional poliomyelitis eradication plan endorsed by the regional committee. It then reports progress in the Western Pacific Region, including China's provincial and county coverage targets being met early in most surveyed provinces and higher coverage in the Lao People's Democratic Republic after an intensive campaign in Vientiane.

sections.extract: 1 ره 1 A42/10 صفحة ‎١١‏ 11 28م الموسع للتمنيع مع الرعاية الصحية الأولية في جميع البلدان تقريبا ‎٠‏ وهناك دلائل كشثيرة على أن خدمات التمنيع تقدم في معظم المرافق الصحية سواء منها التابعة للقطاع العام أو القطاع الخاص ‎٠‏ 1-5 وقد تحقق التعجيل داخل الاقليم عن طريق التعاون الأفضل بين القطاعات والتعبكة الاجتماعية الفعالة ‎٠‏ وكان الالتزام من جانب القادة السياسيين والزعماء الدينيين وغيرهم من العوامل الكبيرة الأهمية ‎٠‏

sections.title: Page 12

summary.text: Reports gains in fully immunized children and disease surveillance in the Philippines, and describes vaccine supply in the Western Pacific Region, with China producing all EPI vaccines, Viet Nam producing some vaccines below WHO standards or in insufficient quantity, and the Philippines self-sufficient in BCG and tetanus toxoid. It notes the transfer of hepatitis B vaccine technology from Japan to China, plasma-derived vaccine work for Tonga, Samoa and Fiji, and a regional resolution to eradicate poliomyelitis, with many countries reporting no cases for years. It then begins a section on remaining obstacles to the 1990 goal, arguing that the outlook is encouraging because coverage now rests on infrastructure built through an early focus on training and step-by-step expansion.

sections.title: Page 13

summary.text: Notes that most developing countries only had adequate immunization infrastructure from the mid-1980s, and that most unimmunized or partly immunized infants live not in Africa but in five large countries—India, China, Nigeria, Bangladesh and Indonesia—with a third in India alone. It discusses the outlook for these countries and for a few others with very low coverage, such as Bangladesh and Ethiopia, and includes a figure showing the share of unimmunized infants by country group.

sections.title: Page 14

summary.text: Presents a figure comparing the highest reported coverage with a third dose of oral polio vaccine or DPT in developing countries with the coverage projected for the end of 1990. It sets out the assumed increases behind these projections for the five largest developing countries, the next group of large countries, and all other developing countries.

sections.extract: A42/10 1 ٠١/52ج‎ صفحة ‎١٤‏ 14 28م 8-5 ويقدم الشكل ؟ تقديرات لما يمكن توقعه في البلدان النامية بنهاية عام ‎٠ 111١‏ ويرتكز هذا الشكل على أعلى تغطية ‎٠‏ بالنسبة لجرعة ثالثة من اللقاح الفموي المضاد لفيروس السنجابية أو من اللقاح الثلاثي » تم التبليغ عنها في كانون الأول/ ديسمبر ‎١1848‏ وأسقطت ( بالتقدير الذاتي ) حتى نهاية عام +١٩٩ ء بما في ذلك التغطية بلقاح الحصبة ولقاح بي سي جي بالاضافة الى اللقاح المضاد لفيروس السنجابية

sections.title: Page 15

summary.text: Argues that with strong effort developing-country coverage could rise substantially by the end of 1990, that high coverage targets lay the groundwork for reducing and eradicating diseases in the next decade, and that many children who receive a first dose never return for later ones. It highlights missed opportunities when eligible children brought to health facilities for illness are not immunized, citing the Gambia's integrated curative and preventive care, and explains why measles coverage lags behind other vaccines, partly because vaccination is generally not given before nine months of age. It also notes low tetanus toxoid coverage of pregnant women and calls for better performance of existing staff and facilities through training, clear responsibilities and supervision.

sections.extract: A42/10 ٠١/5 ‏ج1‎ صفحة ‎١٥‏ 5 86م ه١٠‏ ومن ثم فانه يمكن » ببذل جهود قوية » التوصل بنهاية عام ‎١٩٩٠+‏ الى تغطية نسبتها نحو ه'* ؛ والاسقاطات تنطوي دائما على خطر ‎٠‏ فالبعض يعتبرها مفرطة في التفاؤل والبعض الآخر يتوقع أداء أفضل أيضا ‎٠‏ وينبغي ‎٠‏ على أية حال . محاولة بلوغ مرامي تغطية نسبتها ‎86٠١‏ لأنها تهيئء الوضع المناسب لعمليات الخفض والازالة والاستكصال المقترح تحقيقها في العقد المقبل ‎٠‏ وفي-جميع البلدان تقريبا »

sections.title: Page 16

summary.text: Stresses the role of community action and mobilization, cautioning that campaign-style efforts such as national immunization days must not undermine permanent health services, and warns that many developing countries will need sustained external support well into the twenty-first century. It gives simplified cost estimates showing that external needs, including for the poliomyelitis eradication initiative, remain small in the context of development aid, and recalls development agencies' assurance at Bellagio that funds would be available if countries made immunization a priority.

sections.extract: A42/10 ٠/1 ‎١٦‏ 6 ع286م ‏ه1١‏ والعمل المجتمعي ضروري أيضا ‎٠‏ وذلك أنه يمكن لأعضاء المجتمع تحديد الأطفال المؤهلين للتمنيع وتوجيههم الى خدمات التمنيع ‎٠‏ ويمكن لاأعضاء المجتمع أيضا أن يمارسوا الضغط اللازم لتوفير خدمات التمنيع في الأوقات والاماكن المناسبة للمجتمع وليس للعامل الصحي فقط ‎٠‏ ويستطيع المجتمع اليقظ أن يمارس الضغط السياسي اللازم لضمان توفير مجموعة شاملة من خدمات الرعاية الصحية الأولية » بما في ذلك التمنيع

sections.title: Page 17

summary.text: Notes that external funding has so far largely kept pace with needs but that the poliomyelitis eradication initiative requires a sharp rise in extrabudgetary resources, which the programme has already begun to commit at some risk to routine support, and opens a section on actions needed towards 2000, starting with raising and sustaining coverage and shifting the focus to controlling the six target diseases. It describes the World Health Assembly's 1988 mandate to eradicate polio by 2000 and how the global plan of action was drafted and refined through consultations with national programme managers, regional staff and WHO headquarters units.

sections.extract: A42/4210 ٠ ١ ‏ج11/‎ صفخة ‎١/‏ 7 ع28م 5؟؟ وقد واكب التمويل الخارجي للبرنامج الموسع للتمنيع » حتى الآن ؛ الاحتياجات الى حد بعيد ‎٠‏ بيد أن مبادرة استتصال التهاب سنجابية النخاع وضعت أعباء فورية على الموارد الخارجة عن الميزانية » التي تلزم زيادتها من مستواها الحالي البالغ نحو ه ملايين دولار أمريكي الى مستوى يتراوح بين ‎١٥‏ مليون و *؟2 مليون دولار أمريكي في السنة تقريبا ‎٠‏ وانطلاقا من توقع ورود هذه الأموال قريبا » بدأ

sections.title: Page 18

summary.text: Lists further consultations on the poliomyelitis eradication plan of action, notes that it has already served as a framework for regional eradication plans, and sets out its main strategies: high immunization coverage in every district, better surveillance and outbreak response, stronger laboratory capacity, public awareness, information for parents and communities, improved rehabilitation services and research. It gives the estimated external resources needed for eradication, compares them with the cost of smallpox eradication, and states that overall EPI external resources will have to rise during the 1990s.

sections.extract: جا 4210 سلمة ‎١٨‏ 8 عهدم - الاستعراضات والمناقشات المفصلة التي جرت خلال مشاورة غير رسمية للخبراء العالميين في مجال التهاب سنجابية النخاع » عقدت في جنيف في 5و1 أيكول /سبتمبر ممكخاء, - الاستعراض الاضافي الذي أجرته المجموعة الاستشارية العالمية للبرنامج الموسع للتمنيع ( حضر اجتماعها مستشارو البرنامج الموسع للتمنيع من كل الاقاليم ) خلال اجتماعها المعقود في الفترة ١-١؟‏ تشرين ن الأول/ أكتوبر ٩٨٨ * 5-7 وترد خطة العمل في

sections.title: Page 19

summary.text: Calls for larger contributions to the EPI special account to support poliomyelitis eradication and stresses that measles and neonatal tetanus also need intensified control. It notes that measles still kills roughly a million children a year, describes research on a measles vaccine strain that might be given at six months and a target to cut reported cases sharply, and links neonatal tetanus elimination to safe motherhood through immunization and clean delivery. It also discusses introducing new or improved vaccines, such as those against yellow fever, hepatitis B and Japanese encephalitis, and using the EPI to promote other primary health care measures such as nutrition, diarrhoeal disease control, birth spacing and vitamin A and iodine supplementation.

summary.text: Describes research and development as a major EPI priority for the 1990s, recalling early work adapting the cold chain and introducing time–temperature indicators, and the creation of an EPI research and development group funded by the Rockefeller Foundation, UNDP and later the Netherlands, with a focus on applied research. The conclusion states that the programme is fulfilling its promise, has made immunization a recognized national and international priority, and needs continued support for disease control and eradication, new vaccines and other primary health care work on the way to health for all by 2000.

The introduction recalls the 1988 World Health Assembly commitment to eradication, the Talloires Declaration issued by the Task Force for Child Survival, and the plan's grounding in the experience of the Region of the Americas.

sections.title: Page 25

summary.text: Explains the grounds for optimism about poliomyelitis eradication, including rising immunization coverage, the need for better surveillance, the role of dense urban areas in spreading wild poliovirus, a possibly lower risk of re-established transmission in freed areas, and the fact that only a small share of estimated cases is reported, so improved surveillance may make incidence seem to rise. It stresses that strategies and budget estimates must stay flexible and sets the targets for 2000: no clinical polio associated with wild virus, no wild poliovirus found anywhere in community or environmental samples, and the start of independent certification of global eradication.

sections.title: Page 26

summary.text: Sets interim poliomyelitis eradication targets for 1995, including interrupting wild poliovirus transmission in the European and Western Pacific Regions with certification in the Americas, stopping transmission in at least five countries in each of the African, Eastern Mediterranean and South-East Asia Regions, expanding the laboratory network and reviewing national plans annually. It then lists targets for 1990, such as district-level monitoring of incidence and coverage, monthly reporting, eradication plans in endemic countries, vaccines meeting WHO requirements and a standard case definition and laboratory methods.

sections.title: Page 27

summary.text: Continues the 1990 targets for poliomyelitis eradication, covering training materials for field and laboratory staff, a network of reference laboratories, simple rapid tests, epidemiological research, review of oral vaccine formulations and development of new vaccines, and regional advisory bodies to review progress and foster cooperation among supporters. It then introduces the strategies section, naming seven key areas: immunization coverage, surveillance, laboratory services and vaccine quality control, training, social mobilization, rehabilitation services, and research and development.

sections.title: Page 28

summary.text: Sets the coverage strategy for the first period: all countries should reach at least 80% polio vaccine coverage among infants and children aged one to four, with higher levels likely needed in dense urban slums, backed by training, supervision, fewer missed opportunities and better social communication. On surveillance, it calls for monthly district reporting that includes reports of zero cases, a move to weekly reporting as eradication nears, a standard case definition based on acute flaccid paralysis, and expert review committees to classify cases as vaccine-associated, wild imported, wild indigenous or unknown.

sections.title: Page 29

summary.text: Describes strategies to strengthen laboratory capacity through an expanded network of reference laboratories and specimen exchange, to ensure all programmes use vaccines meeting WHO requirements with good cold-chain management, and to revise training materials for health workers and laboratory staff. It also covers social mobilization to sustain political and financial commitment through media messages, educational materials and political, religious and community leaders, and the use of the eradication effort to strengthen rehabilitation services in developing countries.

sections.title: Page 30

summary.text: Explains how rehabilitation work supports eradication by helping ensure all cases become known, cites international efforts by IMPACT and Rotary International, and sets research priorities such as rapid diagnostic tests, detecting wild poliovirus in the environment, operational research on reaching urban slum populations, and better oral polio vaccine formulations. It then outlines the phases for 1991–1995, when health workers in all countries not yet polio-free are trained and reliable monthly district surveillance is in place, and 1996–2000, when the global drive intensifies and remaining transmission should be confined to a limited number of countries.

summary.text: Notes that in the final phase some countries will need extraordinary measures such as national or local immunization campaigns, as well as extra external funding and international advisers, and explains how national eradication plans should group countries or areas into four categories by reported cases and immunization coverage. It details the actions for group A (polio-free countries), group B (few cases and high coverage) and group C (more cases with moderate coverage), covering continued immunization, zero reporting, case investigation, laboratory confirmation, expert review committees and outbreak control.

It gives the share of world population in each group and begins the section on WHO's responsibilities, stressing technical leadership, broad collaboration with partners, and coordination through the EPI Global Advisory Group and existing national and regional mechanisms.

summary.text: Lists the tasks of WHO regional offices, such as technical support and coordination, regional plans of action based on national programme reviews, support for national managers, emphasis on surveillance and reference laboratory services, computer software for management information systems and training of national laboratory staff, with yearly review of regional progress by advisory bodies and periodic review by regional committees. It then sets out the global functions of the Expanded Programme on Immunization, including leading resource mobilization and donor coordination, preparing training prototypes, improving surveillance and evaluation methods, updating global data, strengthening vaccine quality control and vaccine development, and building a network of polio reference laboratories.

summary.text: Completes WHO's global responsibilities with annual review of the poliomyelitis eradication initiative and certification of eradication, then opens the resource requirements section with an estimate of the cost of fully immunizing children in developing countries, the expected share of external support and the need for partners to increase their contributions. It notes the extra annual extrabudgetary support needed at WHO headquarters for eradication, excluding the separately funded Americas, and begins describing the need for international staff to assess, plan, monitor and evaluate national programmes.

sections.title: Page 39

summary.text: Budgets research and development for improved laboratory diagnostic tests, operational research on cost-effective ways to stop wild poliovirus transmission, field studies on the best oral polio vaccine formulation and development of improved vaccines, and gives the total resources needed for the first period. It then outlines how needs will change in 1991–1995, with more national evaluation, national staff, travel, laboratory and research support, and in 1996–2000, when intensive eradication strategies and personnel costs are expected to rise further.

sections.title: Page 40

summary.text: Annex table summarizing the additional EPI resources required for poliomyelitis eradication by programme component and period, covering staff, meetings, monitoring and surveillance, training, laboratory support and research and development. The figures are almost entirely garbled in the OCR, and a footnote states that the table excludes the external resources needed for routine EPI operations.
